newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire conflict uproots refugees, some go to Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Zaire conflict uproots refugees, some go to Rwanda.

text.p: Warfare between ethnic Tutsi rebels and Zairean government troops has forced up to half a million Rwandan Hutus to flee refugee camps just inside eastern Zaire, with some going back to Rwanda despite fear of persecution, aid workers said on Sunday.

Most refugees have trekked deeper into Zaire but aid workers said at least 1,500 crossed on Sunday to Rwanda, where the Hutu refugees are afraid of persecution or punishment for the mass killing of Rwandan Tutsis in 1994 by Hutus.
More than one million Rwandan Hutu refugees have lived in a string of camps in eastern Zaire since the 1994 genocide, in which Hutu mobs and militia also killed moderate Hutus.
Aid workers said that over the weekend at least four people died in an attack on Kibumba camp and one Zairean guard was killed and three wounded in an attack on Katale camp.
The head of the U.N. refugee agency, UNHCR, on Sunday called on combatants to stop attacking refugees and to open corridors for those caught in the fighting.

UNHCR chief Sadako Ogata, raising the spectre of an even worse tragedy in store, said: "A catastrophe greater than the one we knew in 1994 is what worries me most. I appeal to the combatants: please spare the refugees and local populations."
Many ordinary Zaireans say Hutus and Tutsis have exported their problems to Zaire and they want to be left in peace.

An unemployed teacher in Bukavu, the lakeside town in the path of advancing Tutsi rebels, told Reuters: "International opinion must persuade the Hutus and Tutsis to solve their problems themselves and not here on Zairean soil."
Michele Quintaglie of the World Food Programme said that about 1,500 Rwandans had crossed into Rwanda from Zaire and were now at the Nkamira waystation near the town of Gisenyi.
Speaking by telephone from the Ugandan capital Kampala, she said about 3,000 Zaireans had also fled to Rwanda.
Most of the Rwandan refugees preferred to head west.
A stream of about 200,000 fled westward after one of eastern Zaire's biggest camps was reported to have been shelled from Rwanda on Saturday and several refugees were killed.
"There is a stream of people about 25 km (15 miles) long...I saw pregnant women, handicapped people, little children," U.N. official Panos Moumtzis said from the Zairean town of Goma.
Moumtzis, a UNHCR spokesman, told Reuters that refugees said sustained artillery attacks on the Kibumba camp had come from the direction of Rwanda.

"We saw four dead bodies in Kibumba, but refugees told us there were a lot more dead...We were told there were at least 100 wounded," said Moumtzis, who visited the now abandoned camp 25 km (15 miles) north of Goma on Sunday morning.
The refugees are on the move after a series of attacks by Tutsi rebels fighting Zairean troops in eastern Zaire.
The rebels, from the 300,000-strong Banyamulenge community that migrated 200 years ago from what is now Rwanda to Zaire, are resisting orders to quit Zaire.
The armies of both Rwanda and Burundi, Zaire's small neighbours to the east, are dominated by the Tutsi minorities and diplomats fear they are being drawn into the conflict.

A central objective for both countries is the closure of the Hutu refugee camps located right on their borders and used as bases for Hutu rebel infiltrators. This objective is being achieved by the past fortnight's fighting.
Zaire says Rwanda is sending troops to support Tutsi rebels, a charge Rwanda denies.

Moumtzis said the refugees who had fled Kibumba were being directed to a camp at Mugunga 13 km (eight miles) west of Goma. "About 5,000 refugees an hour are entering Mugunga," he said, adding that U.N. staff with loudspeakers were telling refugees not to enter Goma city.

Eighteen aid workers on Sunday flew out of Goma in a U.N. plane after the Zairean authorities briefly closed the airport, Stromberg said. From Bukavu, a 27-seater plane evacuated French and Italian nationals without incident on Sunday.
Bukavu was tense as the sound of distant cannon fire from the south echoed round the town, and Zairean troops, recently reinforced, were noticeably nervous.
